And then in the later days, Lee Collins used to play there. But you never worked there with Lee? No, I didn't work there with Lee. Lee and I worked together on a kidney job there. I was a real man born in Burgundy. Call it E-Likes.

Let me get back to this end of time this time. When you first went there, that was the band they had there and they weren't using it after. No. And you went there and played a little. Did you join the band or just?

No, I just played with them that night. And, as a matter of fact, they hired me to play clarinet. And when I got there, I played a few numbers on the clarinet and they asked me could I play the sax? I told them I don't know how to play some numbers on it. And they asked me what key. I told them what key. And they're too hard and I told them. And I've been tearing out everything.

When you first started playing the saxophone, did you try to make the same kind of thing that you were making on the clarinet? Some of them, yeah. I mean, it wasn't a completely new style of playing for you? No, no, no. Some of them I was making on the clarinet. And did you, after you, this sounds funny, after you started playing the sax, did you ever try to make anything on the clarinet that you've been making on the sax? No. You never did that? No. And you never do that now? No. No. I mean, you play clarinet now, you don't play it like you, you don't ever think you've got a sax there. I mean, you always played like the clarinet line. Yeah, I don't play sax in the sax. So what was the first band you really joined on the sax?
The first band I really joined playing saxophone was my own band. Handis, Louisiana, Shakers.
How did you get that band together? How did you get that band together?

Well, that's kind of a mystery. Let me see, I was playing up at Seven and Howard. And it's, uh, Smiley and Joe. Now, I can't think of his trumpet player's name. But he's out in California. I don't know. Anyway, that's where I was playing. Ridgely's brother was managing the Pelican Garden. And he was in there one night. And he heard me playing. And he called me off to stand. I went to his table. We had a couple of drinks. And he asked me, he said, Andy, why don't you get up a band and come play for me? I said, play for you. I said, where you got to play? He said, I manage the Pelican. I said, oh yeah? He said, yeah. He said, I can give you three full nights a month. Two of them, I said, well, what kind of band do you want there? He said, well, we only use big bands there. Eight to ten pieces of it. So, I told him I'd see him in a couple of days. Well, I did. I went and seen him. And, uh, I went and talked to several fellas and got them together. Told him the proponents of it. And, um, I went and bought the music. No, just, you know, just copies of orchestrations. I bought about ten or fifteen of them. And we met at the Pelican and went up there and locked the doors and we started wrestling with that music. And we got it down pretty good. What year was that? I was around thirty-two. And then, uh, we played there. From there I went to, uh, Bugalooza's, oh, numerous of times I played in Bugalooza's, a big band, at that big club there.
How many pieces you said it was?
Ten.
Remember who the men were?

Well, I had, uh, one time I had, uh, Alvin Alcorn on trumpet. Was that in the beginning, I mean, when you first formed? Yes. Yeah? I had, uh, Willie Pardew on second trumpet. And I had, uh, Lee Collins on third trumpet. I had, uh, Raymond Brown on trombone. Uh-huh. I had David Jones on tenor sax. I was playing fourth, I was playing fourth, Alton, Bodley on third, Alton. Who was that? Bodley. Bodley? Yeah. I don't remember him. Well, him and H.E. was raised up together. Was that his first name or second name? No, that was his, I think that was his last name. Uh-huh. I had H.E. on guitar. Old Man Kimball on bass, tuba. Uh-huh. Raymond, uh, what's Raymond's name? Brown. Piano player. Doris. Raymond Doris on, uh, on piano. Uh-huh. And who did you head on drums? Roy E.
Oh, uh-huh.

Yeah, that's true. Well, I played there a long time. I left there and went to Shreveport. Played two nights engaging in Shreveport. Left there and I went to Bournemouth. Played two nights there. Went to Euston. Played two nights there. Went to Wichita Falls. Played one night there. Jumped back to Folkwood. Played two nights there. And come back in. But that time I had 22 passengers bus then. Yeah? What, a band bus? Yeah. 22 passengers bus on my own chauffeur.
Yeah?
Yeah, at that time.

They had the band knife on the side of the bus? Yeah. What was the knife on the side of the bus? Handis, Louisiana Shakers. Handis or John Handis? No, Handis or John Handis. You keep the same men in the band in that tub? Yeah. Was there any chance? No, the same men.

When I come back here, Don Albert took Alvin from me. He had a regular job, I think. Alvin Alcorn went with him. And a trombone player. He went with him. And somebody just kept streaming out of the band. And he left and went with Don Albert.
Who was your top player on in the... I don't remember.
David Jones.
David Jones. One of them.
He had a music school here. He still got one in California. Yeah, he's got a... He was...

Let me just ask you one thing about the Pelican that I meant to ask you. You say you had three or four nights a month there. Yeah. That's all you had, three or four nights a month? Yeah. So it was one night a week, huh?

Yeah, maybe one night a week, yeah. Did you keep filling in with other jobs with that? Well, yeah, yeah. I guess you have to. We kept filling in with other jobs. The first man met... Ben met Earl Heinz's band when he came down here. At this time. Yeah, and he had a troubled band. Yeah, I met him when he came down here. And met... Clayborne Williams. What do you mean met him? You played opposite of what? Yeah, I played opposite. I played on one standing, then played on the other. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Well, that was most people that had been on the Pelican, though, when Clayborne played. Whose band did they like best? Well, I don't know. He had his father's and I had mine. Both of them. I don't know.
So who did you get into the band when Don Albert took, Albert and what you call him?

I got trumpet player downtown. He's a plasterer. I can't think of his name now, but he could never play nothing but the music. He couldn't get off of nothing. But he was a fine musician. Is he still around? Yeah, he's still around.
What does he look like?

He's a little brown-skinned fellow. Slender. I can't think of his name now. But anyway. Who did he play with? I think they had a band right here. He used to call it a Creosa or something like that. He used to play with them. I don't know who that was. I don't know who that was. Yeah, he used to play with them.
I wanted to ask you, did you ever play in the Pine Tree Inn?

Pine Tree Inn. Where is that? In Bungalus. Yeah. Yeah, I just wondered. I was thinking about the places out there, you know. Yeah, I played. I played. Yeah, that's where Jim Cool was playing with it at night. And the fellow running to him and skylocking, and running to him and knocked his horn out of his hand on the floor, and they stepped on it. Stepped right on the slide, boy. And it was no more good. Playing. Playing.
So you still kept these, uh, just trying to piece band together for a while?
Wait a minute. Did the guy play for his horn or that? Mm-hmm. He didn't care, huh?

Walked out. We got the manager, the guy was giving the dance. He seemed, he claimed he's trying to trace him, but he never did. He didn't care about it. He didn't care about it. I think it's that. Mm-hmm. I'll take it. Yeah, he never did. He didn't care about it. Jim had to buy him another one. Yeah, I kept the band on the Pelican for quite a while. I stayed there about two years or something. And then, uh, meanwhile, uh, back in, uh, in the 20s, I went on the boat and played with Feed Marble out there for, uh, five, six days I played out there with him, especially tracking the clarinet. Because when I was playing at the entertainers, old man Stretford and his brother and Faith used to come outside and sit on the automobile and listen to me play. Mm-hmm. And, uh, yeah, Faith to hire me for five nights out there. I went out there for the Faith to play for those five nights. Well, like a guest artist? Yeah.
Did they have your name up? You know, did they advertise you were playing there as guest artist? No. No.

No, they didn't even advertise. Not as I can remember. But anyway, uh, this guy, Charlie Crest was playing, uh, accordion with Faith, the us at that time. And, uh, he got back to St. Louis. He had his own band. And, uh, he said for me to come up there, but I didn't go that time. Uh, because I had too much work in the owners. I couldn't leave. I mean, I had too many contracts signed. I couldn't leave. So, uh, so about six, eight months after he come down here, with Faith again, and the farm and then told me he had a spot for me up there and asked me what I'd be interested in. So we talked it over and they offered me $115 a week for the century. So I took the job. I went on up there and played at that Democratic Club. I stayed up there with them about a year or something. And then I left there and went to, uh, Thirty-Face of Market. Played for the Italian down there. That's where I met Guy Kelly. Yeah. Mm-hmm. And I played there for him for about eight months I played there. You knew Guy Kelly before though. Oh yeah, I knew Guy. Because I brought Guy from Baton Rouge too and knew all of them to play with me at the entertainers club. And then I'd be playing with him in Baton Rouge. And then I left there and I went to Springfield, Illinois and I stayed there. I didn't stay in San Diego, Illinois too long because I got definitely sick up there. Yeah. Yeah. And I stayed up there, I don't know, about seven months I stayed in Springfield. And then the doctor told me I better get back close to home. So I left there and I come back down here. And I've been back down here.
What did you, uh, you got any questions?
Oh yeah. I never did understand whose band it was up at Seventh and Howard. Seventh and Howard? Yeah, before you went in the Pellet.
It was Smalley and Jewel's band.
And what was he playing then?
He was playing guitar.
And who was in the band?
Lewis Gibbon on piano, Smalley and Jewel, myself. And, uh, I can't think of the trumpet bells name. Mm-hmm. There was four of us. Yeah.
And did they have other bands at the Pelicans or the other nuns?
Oh yeah, yeah, sure. Who would they be selling? Oh, Pop Celestan played up there. Mm-hmm. Rene played there. Mm-hmm. And, uh, Sidney Dezby played there. Oh, they had bands up there. Mm-hmm.
I'm trying to think of that trumpet player who was a class, right? It couldn't have been somebody like Shelley LaMelle or...
No, no, no, no.
Well, we could continue that all night and we don't have time. Okay. You have a clue?
No, go ahead. Well, let me think. I wanted to ask you about when you got into the La Vida dance hall. How did you come by that job? Or was it too much of a jump from where we were? No. Uh...
I was playing there with a fellow by the name of Tink. Piano player. Tink's been there, oh, in quite a number of years. Tink was that Tink? Yeah, but, uh... Yeah.
Tink Batte's was his name?

I don't know his last name. His name was Tink. Well, anyway, I was playing there with him. And, uh, him and the boss got himself gonna misunderstanding or something. And, uh... He asked me could I bring him a piano player? I said, well, we got a piano player. He said, no, Tink quit tonight. I said, yeah, I'll get your piano player if he quit. He said, yeah, he quit. He said, yeah, he quit. He told me tonight he quit. I got Joe Rubishow. And put him in there. That's how I got to do it. That's at La Vida. At La Vida. I had, uh... One time I had John Marrera, Albert, uh... Morgan, Joe Rubishow, uh... Crown's Hall, his brother. Not Edwin, I believe the one called Charlie. He was a tenor player too. And myself.
What kind of music did you have to play out there?

Well, we had to play practical all types. We had to play some slow numbers, some mediums, some fast, and some waltzes. I guess we'd play around, oh, eight, nine waltzes a night. We were more than that. Because every fourth of them, you had to play a waltz. You'd play a waltz, and you'd play a fast number, medium, or a slow drag, and then a waltz. That routine all night long, every fourth of them, you had to play a waltz. What hours you worked at? Oh, one hour. I mean, you go to work at eight, and you get off at one, end of the week. On Saturday, you go to work at eight, you get off at two, or two-thirty. As long as somebody was in there, they wanted you to play. You didn't have no union or nothing, I think, to stop you. So they actually play on, they used to play. Two-thirty. Huh. And then the business thing about that, when we get off, I mean, there's no stopping. No stopping in 10 minutes like that. Yeah. One number right, one right behind the other. What a one? Yeah. You have any breaks at all? No. You didn't even have a break to eat. One man eat at a time. He didn't play much organist, because Black Benny was a more street man parade man.

Were you playing clarinet at this time of tour, or just all around to? Where? Well, around this time, did you pick up the clarinet once in a while, or all in a while? No. I mean, when you light the clarinet down, you more or less light it down. Forgot it. Yeah.
Forgot it, because everybody wanted the altitude. Nobody wanted the clarinet. Everybody wanted the altitude. Yeah. I forgot the clarinet. I got the clarinet down in 1928.
Did you have a band with Kid Howell and Jim Crow? Yeah. Who else was in that band? Uh,

Miss Howard, Jim Crow, Drew Rubishow. I think John Burrell was playing that, and myself. I don't know how many of those are. Did you have the drums or bass? Yeah, we had drums and trying to sing. Where's the band coming from? I don't know if it's in the... Alfred. Oh, Alfred Whittemey. That's the playing drums. Then Howard and I had a band together.
Yeah?
Yeah. What, after La Vida? No. After we left with La Vida,
we had a band together. Whose band was it when you were playing at La Vida with Howard and Jim in the band? Whose band was that? It was my band. Your band? Yeah. Yeah, it was my band.

Can I get back to the early days for a minute? Yeah, sure. When I'm interested in what I die, say in the 20s, how would they get a brass band to bury them there? Would they hire an organized band always over the days? How about band or what?

Well, in the early 20s when the musicians would die, most musicians would volunteer to play. You didn't have to have no money. Most of them would volunteer to play. And that was fun for them to get out there and play for the funeral.
Did you play many?

Yeah. You see, the funeral and those days last all day. It'd bury around nine, ten o'clock in the morning, be five, six o'clock in the evening before you get back home. And you'd be studied playing, go every way. Just walking and playing. I mean, everybody was young and full of life and they'd just go in and play. A lot of times we used to go better, man. And on our way back, we'd pick up four or five musicians, come to meet you, playing.
Would you have any written music at that kind of funeral or would it be all head stuff?
All head stuff.
Who would be some of the guys that would do that a lot? That you played with, you know?

Well, it'd be all mixed up around there. Jordan McCullough, he'd be playing sometime. Shots, he'd play some. Sometimes Chris would play. Randy would play. Very seldom, what do you call them, play the trombone play because he was couldn't do much walking or yank. He couldn't do much walking around. But Jim would play. And another fellow, George Washington, he was a trombone player. A little bit of guy, about that high. He would play.
How high, about four feet, five feet?

He was a little bit taller than Dad. George Washington. The world's largest midget, I guess. He used to follow shoes a lot. Him and the trumpet player by the name Amos White used to play for the shoes a lot.
Could George Washington reach down for a seventh position in the trombone? Because they aren't so long enough?

I wouldn't know. That's funny. But he was a good trombone player. What he couldn't make down in a seventh position, he'd make up in the first or the third. I imagine his arms wasn't long enough to reach down there. Not where we go from here. What?
Well, we didn't get after Springfield, Illinois. If you got sick and you came back, what happened then?

Well, I come in, I opened up a restaurant and a ball. Uh-oh. Right across the track there. And I stayed around here about two and a half years. You play anything? No, I couldn't play nothing. I had a bad stomach, I couldn't do nothing. I left and went back to New Orleans. And that's where I started playing again. With who? With different fellas.

You were spotting there for a while, right? Yeah, different fellas I was playing with. What about some of the musicians from out of town that you used to play with, you know, that would come down here and maybe be playing with the Lyric or someplace like that? Who would some of them be? I don't know. Well, you must have played with some real famous guys. I don't know if you told me about them.
That's somewhere.
What about, uh, Fat Wallace? You ever know him? Sure, I know Fat. You play with him much? No.

Jam or anything? Oh yeah, I jam with him. Yeah. Oh yeah, I jam with him. When he coming out of the lyrics, the lyrics to you. Yeah, I jam with him. Did you ever get any offers from those guys? Yes, in my twenties I got a lot of offers. Who were some of the guys? Jimmy Lundford. I got offers from Jimmy. There's another guy named Boy, I can't think of his name now. He come to me directly. Yeah, well. And then late years you played a lot of grass band work on Hope too, wasn't it? Yeah, I played with, uh, but there wasn't a lot of time for that. That was with John Casney. Yeah. Tuxedo band. Anybody else? Well, I played a few jobs with, uh, uh, to New Rica. There was about the only two brass bands I played with.

But in the early years you weren't in brass bands, my general. Not a lot, huh? Not a lot, no. Not a regular amount, that's what I'm trying to say. No, no, no. Did we get into the 40s during the war? Where were you doing? Wait, where did that La Vida business come in? That's after you came back from here, after your restaurant and bar here? The La Vida?
The La Vida? Or La Vida? No, the La Vida come in after I come from Bad News.
So it was before you had the restaurant and bar?
Oh, yes, yes.
And then you went back in the field and you walked after that? That's right, yeah. And you've been gigging around ever since, huh? Ever since. Ever since. Thank you.
